newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Western insurers vital as Asia develops.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Western insurers vital as Asia develops.

text.p: Western firms are crucial to the development of domestic Asian insurance markets but attempting to directly transplant a blueprint from the West to the East would fail, a top industry executive said.
"It would be a fatal mistake," said Ian Rickard, managing director of the Singapore unit of Lincoln National Reinsurance Co.
"If there are blueprints, they have to be very flexible," he told Reuters in an interview at the weekend.

"The fundamentals of insurance do not alter dramatically from one continent to the next, but the manner and method of operation and the way in which things are accepted by markets are very, very different.
"You have to synthesise the international experience and make it come out in a manner that is acceptable in the local context," Rickard said.
Lincoln National gained full approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, for its life and health underwriting branch operation in the city state in February.

"The upside for regulators allowing foreign participation is our knowledge of technology, distribution and development of appropriate products designed to suit the domestic environment," Rickard said.
For fledgling insurance companies, forging alliances to provide expertise and experience to foster an open market culture is the main route forward.

"New and emerging companies need to be in a position to effectively participate in the market. Not only is it important for us to provide risk transfer ability, but also to be able to work with them from the very earliest stages to make sure they meet their goals," Rickard said.

This was especially true in life and health business, where insurance was needed to back private health care and help Asian governments avoid the burden of state-run health schemes in Europe and the United States that eat into budgets, he said.

"From the health point of view, governments are recognising the costs of health care and not wanting to go down the same route as the European economies have done with governments assuming too much responsibility for the costs," Rickard said.
And with international experience in this area, the introduction of private sector care operations will be far more rapid in Asia than it was in the West.
"What took 15 to 20 years to happen in the U.S. will take probably five years here," Rickard said.
